prerequisites: Complete courses 1.6–1.12: the course 1.6 PKI with its SBD Computer Authentication template and the SBD Certificate Autoenrollment GPO at the domain root, SBD-DHCP01 (course 1.7), whose relay course 1.7 verified, the three administration seats (course 1.8), and the logging pipeline (courses 1.10–1.12), on the network's routed, segmented VLANs.
Prepare a patched Windows client reference image (or template) for the fifty endpoints, obtained through the approved offline media process.

Confirm the Workstations OU and the computer redirect from course 1.5, and the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy objects (GPOs) for your Windows client release, imported in course 1.5 from the package course 1.4 staged and still unlinked there. Have course 1.4's media set at hand — SCC, the Windows client STIG and its SCAP benchmark, with connected-side-hashes.csv — for SBD-ADMIN-PC01's own SCC copy in lesson 7.

Confirm the VLAN 80 access switch supports 802.1X port authentication, including a monitor (audit) mode that logs each result without blocking traffic. No new server is needed: the Network Policy Server (NPS) role goes on SBD-DHCP01.
labNote: Fifty endpoints join a network that is finally ready for them: addressed by DHCP, landed by OU redirect, hardened by policy at first boot, certified by autoenrollment, and watched by the pipeline from their first sign-in. Tier 0 steps run from AdminJumpBox01, Tier 1 steps on SBD-DHCP01 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and Tier 2 steps inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01; each seat keeps its part of the record under C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet. The sample names run SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC50; match them to your own plan.

DISA · STIG Group Policy Objects package
Microsoft · Use Windows Event Forwarding to help with intrusion detection

lessons.title: Prepare the fleet rollout
lessons.summary: Fifty of anything needs a factory, not fifty craft projects. Settle the image, the names, the join account, and the policy links so every endpoint is born identical — then prove it on paper before proving it on metal.
objectives: Finalize the reference image and naming plan for fifty endpoints.
Create a least-privilege join account scoped to the Workstations OU.
Link the Windows client STIG policies, the local Administrators policy and the workstation firewall policy to the Workstations OU before any join.
steps: Finalize the Windows client reference image: current patches via the approved media process, no preinstalled extras, one local administrator account for Windows LAPS to manage (the Windows client STIG disables the built-in Administrator), and a generalized state so each clone takes its own identity. Record the image version and hash — it is the fleet's common ancestor and belongs in evidence.
Write the naming and rollout plan: SBD-PC01–SBD-PC50, addressed by the course 1.7 DHCP scope, joined in waves (pilot of three, then batches) rather than all fifty at once.

From AdminJumpBox01, create a dedicated domain-join account delegated only Create Computer objects on the Workstations OU — no broader privilege rides along with fifty join operations — and record it beside the same delegation course 1.8 gave SBD Tier 2 Admins for its test client. The course 1.5 redirect already guarantees machines land in that OU. Add a GPO, linked only to the Workstations OU, that makes SBD Tier 2 Admins the managing group in each PC's local Administrators (Group Policy Preferences, Local Users and Groups), as course 1.8 did by hand on its test client; course 1.8's tier logon GPO already denies Tier 0 and Tier 1 sign-ins there.

Link the DISA Windows client policies that course 1.5 imported and left unlinked to the Workstations OU now — the computer policy, the user policy, and course 1.5's loopback (Merge) GPO, as course 1.8 did for Admin Workstations — so the very first pilot boots into the hardened state, and note that the Windows client's own secure defaults will already satisfy some checks, just as Windows Server's did.

Create the workstation firewall GPO (SBD Workstation Firewall in this sample) on the Workstations OU: Windows Defender Firewall on for every profile with inbound traffic blocked by default, and inbound rules that allow Remote Desktop (TCP 3389) and remote management (TCP 5985–5986) only from SBD-ADMIN-PC01 at 10.0.60.30 — the ports its register row, A03, carries. No rule allows SMB or Remote Desktop between workstations: traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router, so this policy, not the core router's rules, enforces the register's peer denies.
lessons.command:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Staging\Windows-client-reference.vhdx
# On AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): the join account's delegation (svc-fleet-join in this sample) and the OU's links
(Get-Acl 'AD:\OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test').Access | Where-Object IdentityReference -match 'svc-fleet-join|SBD Tier 2 Admins' | Select-Object IdentityReference, ActiveDirectoryRights, ObjectType
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
Get-GPOReport -Name 'SBD Workstation Firewall' -ReportType Html -Path C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\workstation-firewall.html
lessons.check: The image is hashed and recorded, the join account holds only Create Computer objects on the Workstations OU, and the client STIG, loopback, local Administrators and firewall GPO links show on that OU, beside course 1.8's tier logon GPO, before any machine exists in it.
lessons.evidence: Keep the image record with its hash, the naming and wave plan, the delegation output for the join account and SBD Tier 2 Admins, the OU's GPO inheritance output, and the firewall GPO report.

quizzes.question: Why does the join account get only create-computer rights on one OU?
answers: Join operations fail with more rights
Fifty joins should carry the least privilege possible — a stolen join credential then creates computer objects, nothing more
Delegation is faster than Domain Admin
quizzes.explanation: Scale multiplies exposure. Scoping the account bounds what the rollout's most-used credential is worth to an attacker.

quizzes.question: Why link the STIG policies before the first machine joins?
answers: So every endpoint's first boot is already the hardened state — no window where an unmanaged machine exists
GPO links expire if unused
The OU cannot be created otherwise
quizzes.explanation: The redirect lands them in the OU, and the pre-linked policy means compliance from minute one — the course 1.5 design, now paying off at scale.

quizzes.question: What makes the reference image part of the evidence?
answers: Images are always evidence
It contains the domain password
Its recorded version and hash are what make fifty 'identical' endpoints a claim you can verify
quizzes.explanation: A configuration record for the fleet starts with the common ancestor. The hash is how an assessor — or future you — confirms descent.

quizzes.question: What stops one workstation from opening SMB or Remote Desktop to another?
answers: The router's access control lists
Each PC's own firewall, set by the workstation firewall GPO — traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router
SBD-DHCP01, which refuses leases to a PC that tries it
quizzes.explanation: Two PCs in VLAN 80 talk through the access switch, so the router never sees their traffic. Each PC's Windows Defender Firewall enforces the register's peer denies, which Inside the Network shows as rules D01 and D02; DHCP only hands out addresses.

recap: One hashed image, one naming plan, waves instead of a big bang.
The join credential can create computer objects and nothing else.
The Workstations OU is armed with policy, and its managers named, before it holds a machine.
Peer SMB and Remote Desktop are blocked by each PC's own firewall, set by policy before the first join.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 joins the pilot and inspects everything a first boot should bring.

lessons.title: Join the pilot and inspect first boot
lessons.summary: Three machines go first, and everything the path has built shows up at once: a DHCP lease through the relay, an OU landing, STIG policy, a DNS record — and the join itself appearing on the analyst's screen.
objectives: Join a three-machine pilot with the scoped account.
Verify lease, OU placement, policy, and DNS registration per machine.
Confirm the joins appear in the logging pipeline.
steps: Deploy SBD-PC01 through SBD-PC03 from the image into VLAN 80 — where the PCs are virtual machines, with the hypervisor's time synchronization turned off, as course 1.3 requires — let each take its DHCP lease, and join sbd.test with the delegated account; nothing about the join should require a privileged credential.

Per machine, verify the inheritance chain: the computer object sits in the Workstations OU (the course 1.5 redirect working), gpresult shows the STIG policies applied, w32tm /query /source names a domain controller, and the A and PTR records SBD-DHCP01 registered for it under svc-dhcp-dns (course 1.7) answer from both DCs.

Confirm the deny side holds: a pilot machine cannot reach another pilot machine's SMB or RDP — the lesson 1 firewall policy refuses it on the destination PC, because traffic inside VLAN 80 never reaches the router — and cannot open anything toward VLAN 60, which the core router's rules deny at the boundary.

Find the three joins in the logging pipeline: the domain controllers' computer-account creation events (4741) should already be on the course 1.10 collector and searchable in SBD-SPLUNK01 (course 1.12) — the first machines this network has watched arrive. If the course 1.10 subscription doesn't carry 4741, add it and record the change.
lessons.command:
Get-ADComputer -SearchBase 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter * | Select-Object Name, DNSHostName
gpresult /r /scope:computer
w32tm /query /source   # a domain controller, never Local CMOS Clock or the hypervisor
Resolve-DnsName SBD-PC01.sbd.test -Server SBD-DC02.sbd.test
Test-NetConnection SBD-PC02.sbd.test -Port 445   # expected: TcpTestSucceeded False
lessons.check: All three pilots sit in the Workstations OU with STIG policy applied, time from a domain controller and DNS registered on both DCs, peer SMB/RDP fails as designed, and the join events are visible in analysis.
lessons.evidence: Keep each pilot's placement, gpresult, time source and DNS proof; the peer-deny output; and the analysis search showing the three computer-account creations.

model.label: Sign in
model.text: A workstation gets its address, finds a domain controller, authenticates, and reads its policy.

quizzes.question: How does a brand-new machine end up hardened without anyone touching it?
answers: Windows hardens itself completely
Redirect lands it in the Workstations OU, where the pre-linked STIG policies apply at first boot
The DHCP server pushes the STIG
quizzes.explanation: Three courses cooperate in that one moment: the course 1.5 redirect, the client policies course 1.5 imported from course 1.4's package, and this course's pre-linked OU.

quizzes.question: Why test pilot-to-pilot SMB and expect failure?
answers: SMB is removed from Windows
The pilots are in different domains
Each PC's firewall policy denies peer SMB and Remote Desktop — lateral movement inside VLAN 80 is cut at the destination host
quizzes.explanation: Peer traffic is switched inside VLAN 80 and never reaches the router, so the register's peer denies (D01 and D02) are enforced by each PC's own firewall — the policy lesson 1 linked before any join.

quizzes.question: What does seeing the joins in analysis demonstrate?
answers: The ordering worked — the pipeline built in courses 1.10–1.12 observed the fleet's very first machines arriving
That Splunk licenses cover 50 hosts
Nothing; joins are not logged
quizzes.explanation: Build the watcher, then the watched. The pilot's appearance on the analyst's screen is the sequencing argument made visible.

recap: Three pilots: leased, landed, hardened, registered — untouched by hand.
Peer traffic fails by design; the denies are the fleet's first evidence.
The pipeline watched the fleet being born.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 gives every endpoint a managed local administrator.

lessons.title: Manage local administrators with Windows LAPS
lessons.summary: Fifty identical machines must not share one local administrator password. Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (Windows LAPS) gives each endpoint its own rotating secret, stored in the directory, readable by the people the tier model says may have it.
objectives: Prepare the directory schema and permissions for Windows LAPS.
Apply the LAPS policy to the Workstations OU.
Retrieve and rotate a managed password under the tier rules.
steps: From AdminJumpBox01, extend the directory schema for Windows LAPS (Update-LapsADSchema, which needs Schema Admins) and grant the Workstations OU's computers the right to update their own password attributes (Set-LapsADComputerSelfPermission) — a one-time Tier 0 action, recorded like any schema change.

Grant read access on the managed passwords to SBD Tier 2 Admins (Set-LapsADReadPasswordPermission) — exactly the people SBD-ADMIN-PC01 exists for. Domain Admins can read them by default; no other group gets the right, and Tier 0 accounts don't sign in on workstations to use one. The tier model decides who may know an endpoint's local secret.

Create the LAPS GPO on the Workstations OU: back up to Active Directory, manage the local administrator account the image carries (named in the policy, because Windows LAPS manages the built-in Administrator unless told otherwise and doesn't create accounts), encrypt the password with SBD Tier 2 Admins as its authorized decryptor (otherwise only Domain Admins can decrypt it), the complexity, length and age the plan sets, and post-authentication actions that reset the password and sign the account out after a short grace period, so a used password does not live on.

On a pilot, confirm the policy applied, retrieve the password from SBD-ADMIN-PC01, use it once, and watch rotation after the grace period — one cycle, fully observed, is the proof the other forty-nine inherit.
lessons.command:
# On AdminJumpBox01 (Tier 0): who holds the LAPS rights on the Workstations OU
Find-LapsADExtendedRights -Identity 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
# Inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (Tier 2)
Get-LapsADPassword -Identity SBD-PC01 -AsPlainText
Get-ADComputer SBD-PC01 -Properties msLAPS-PasswordExpirationTime | Select-Object Name, msLAPS-PasswordExpirationTime
# On the pilot
gpresult /r /scope:computer
lessons.check: The schema holds the LAPS attributes, only SBD Tier 2 Admins (beside the default Domain Admins) can read and decrypt passwords, the policy shows on the pilots, and one retrieve-use-rotate cycle is recorded.
lessons.evidence: Keep the schema-change record, the permission delegation, the LAPS policy report, and the observed rotation cycle.

quizzes.question: What problem does LAPS remove from a fifty-machine fleet?
answers: Slow sign-ins
One shared local administrator password — where a single capture would open every endpoint
Password complexity rules
quizzes.explanation: Identical images tempt identical secrets. Per-machine rotating passwords make one compromised endpoint worth exactly one endpoint.

quizzes.question: Who may read a managed endpoint password?
answers: Any authenticated user
The machine's primary user
SBD Tier 2 Admins, from SBD-ADMIN-PC01 — the tier model decides
quizzes.explanation: LAPS storage is directory data; the reading right is a tiering decision, which course 1.8 already made.

quizzes.question: Why does post-authentication reset matter?
answers: A password that was just used stops being valid — whoever saw it holds an expired secret
It makes passwords longer
It disables the account
quizzes.explanation: The rotation on use closes the window between 'retrieved for support' and 'floating around in a notes file.'

recap: Every endpoint owns its own rotating local secret.
Reading and decrypting rights follow the tier model, from the Tier 2 seat.
One full cycle is observed and on record.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 hands the fleet its certificates.

lessons.title: Autoenroll the fleet's certificates
lessons.summary: Course 1.6 proved autoenrollment on both domain controllers and its pilot, SBD-PKI-MGMT01; this lesson turns it loose. Widen the template permission to a fleet computer group, let the autoenrollment GPO already linked at the domain root do the enrolling, and verify a machine certificate chains and checks revocation across the boundary.
objectives: Widen the computer template's autoenrollment to a fleet computer group.
Confirm hands-free enrollment at Group Policy refresh.
Verify chain and live revocation from an endpoint.
steps: Through the course 1.6 change process (its lesson 8), grant a new computer group — SBD Fleet Computers in this sample, created from AdminJumpBox01 — Read, Enroll and Autoenroll on the SBD Computer Authentication template, from SBD-PKI-MGMT01. Template permissions name groups, never an OU; the change record names the widening and its approver.

Confirm with gpresult that course 1.6's SBD Certificate Autoenrollment GPO, linked at the domain root, already reaches the Workstations OU, then add the pilots to SBD Fleet Computers and restart them so the membership reaches their Kerberos tickets. Watch certificates arrive with no human in the loop: the requests reach SBD-SUBCA01 over the enrollment row course 1.6 confirmed (F23 in this sample).

On an enrolled pilot, export its certificate, clear the URL cache, and run the full verification: the chain must reach the approved root, and the AIA and CDP fetches must answer live from pki.sbd.test through the register's publication row, F18.
Record the issuing CA's view: the issued-certificate log now shows the pilots enrolling — volume the CA was designed for, beginning to arrive, and itself a record worth sampling into evidence.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-PC01, after the restart
gpupdate /force
certutil -pulse
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Select-Object Subject, NotAfter, Thumbprint
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My | Where-Object { $_.EnhancedKeyUsageList.FriendlyName -contains 'Client Authentication' } | Select-Object -First 1 | Export-Certificate -FilePath C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\SBD-PC01.cer
certutil -urlcache * delete
certutil -verify -urlfetch C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\SBD-PC01.cer   # carry the output to SBD-ADMIN-PC01's record
lessons.check: Pilot endpoints enroll hands-free once they are in SBD Fleet Computers, verification passes with live publication retrieval and nothing cached, and the CA's issued log shows their SBD Computer Authentication certificates.
lessons.evidence: Keep the template change record, the SBD Fleet Computers membership, an endpoint's certificate details, the urlfetch output, and a sample of the CA's issued log.

quizzes.question: What governs widening the template from pilot to fleet?
answers: The course 1.6 change process — requester, reviewer, versioning, record
A quick edit on the CA console
Nothing; templates are self-service
quizzes.explanation: The pilot-then-widen plan was written into the template's own record. Scaling it is a change like any other — documented, not improvised.

quizzes.question: What does the endpoint's urlfetch verification exercise, end to end?
answers: Only the local certificate store
Template, CA, DNS alias, publication site, and the registered HTTP path, all in one command
The DHCP relay
quizzes.explanation: One passing verification on a fleet machine is the integration test for everything the PKI path built: course 1.6's hierarchy and publication site, and course 1.2's pki.sbd.test alias.

quizzes.question: Why sample the CA's issued-certificate log into evidence?
answers: Logs expire otherwise
The CA deletes it weekly
What the CA actually signed — and under which template version — is the PKI's ground-truth record
quizzes.explanation: Enrollment at scale is where template mistakes would surface. The issued log is where you would see it, so it joins the record.

recap: The widening went through the change process, not around it.
Enrollment is hands-free for the fleet group and verified live across the boundary.
The CA's issued log joins the evidence.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 puts those certificates to work at the switch port, starting in monitor mode.

lessons.title: Admit only enrolled devices with 802.1X
lessons.summary: Until now, anything plugged into a VLAN 80 port got an address. With 802.1X, the switch asks each machine to prove who it is with the certificate it enrolled. This lesson turns that check on in monitor mode — every result is logged, nothing is blocked yet — because 47 PCs have no certificate until they join the domain; lesson 6 enforces it once the whole fleet has enrolled. No new server: the NPS role joins DHCP on SBD-DHCP01.
objectives: Add the Network Policy Server (NPS) role to SBD-DHCP01 for port authentication.
Configure Extensible Authentication Protocol–Transport Layer Security (EAP-TLS) with machine certificates on the VLAN 80 access ports, in monitor mode.
Prove the pilots authenticate and that NPS logs every result.
steps: Add the Network Policy Server role to SBD-DHCP01 in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, and register it in Active Directory from AdminJumpBox01 (a Tier 0 action: it adds the server to RAS and IAS Servers). Give it an SBD Server Authentication certificate (course 1.6) for SBD-DHCP01.sbd.test, adding SBD-DHCP01 to the SBD TLS Servers group before it requests. It handles port admission only; router logins stay named local accounts, so the server stays in the member-server tier.

Add the VLAN 80 access switch as a RADIUS client with a long, unique shared secret, then create the network policy: wired 802.1X, EAP-TLS only, machine certificates that chain to the approved root and carry the Client Authentication purpose, from the Domain Computers group.

Create quarantine VLAN 90 on the access switch with no gateway and no routes (the core gets no VLAN 90 interface) and set it as the ports' failure and guest VLAN, but enable 802.1X on the VLAN 80 access ports in monitor (audit) mode: the switch runs every authentication and reports the result, yet keeps forwarding on VLAN 80 whatever the outcome (vendors name this mode differently). The other 47 PCs have no machine certificate until they join the domain in lesson 6, so enforcing now would strand them in VLAN 90, with no route to a domain controller. Push the wired 802.1X client settings to the Workstations OU by Group Policy (Wired AutoConfig, EAP-TLS, the approved root as the trusted CA).

Turn on Audit Network Policy Server (success and failure) for SBD-DHCP01 in a separate GPO linked above the STIG GPO, recorded as course 1.10 records audit additions — the STIG's audit policy leaves it off. Then prove monitor mode with the pilots: each authenticates with EAP-TLS and NPS logs a grant (event 6272), while a failed attempt is logged — as event 6273 when the request reaches NPS — but still forwards on VLAN 80. Add register row F20 with its owner, as Inside the Network records it, and confirm the NPS events reach the course 1.10 collector, adding 6272 and 6273 to SBD-ForwardedSecurity's query if it doesn't carry them yet.
lessons.command:
# On an enrolled pilot: the wired interface authenticated with EAP-TLS.
netsh lan show interfaces
# On SBD-DHCP01 (Tier 1): NPS auditing is on, then recent grants (6272) and denials (6273).
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Network Policy Server"
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=6272,6273} -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id
lessons.check: NPS auditing records success and failure; every pilot authenticates with EAP-TLS and NPS logs the grant (6272); a failed authentication is logged but, in monitor mode, the port still forwards on VLAN 80; the ports name VLAN 90 as their failure VLAN; and the NPS events appear in the collector.
lessons.evidence: Keep the network policy export, the RADIUS client list (without the secret), the audit GPO report, the monitor-mode port configuration, the pilots' grant events and the failed test, and the F20 register row.

model.label: SBD-DHCP01
model.text: The NPS role for 802.1X runs here, on the existing DHCP server.

quizzes.question: Once 802.1X is enforced, what lets a workstation onto a VLAN 80 port?
answers: Knowing a shared password
Its machine certificate, checked by NPS through EAP-TLS
Being plugged in before the switch boots
quizzes.explanation: EAP-TLS proves the device holds the private key for a certificate the approved CA issued. No certificate, no access.

quizzes.question: Once enforcement is on in lesson 6, where does an unknown device end up?
answers: Quarantine VLAN 90, which has no routes
VLAN 80, with a warning
The domain controller VLAN, so it can enroll
quizzes.explanation: The failure VLAN gives an unknown device a place to be that leads nowhere: VLAN 90 has no gateway, so nothing it sends is routed.

quizzes.question: Why does NPS on SBD-DHCP01 handle port admission only, not router logins?
answers: NPS cannot authenticate people
Router logins need a separate license
If it authenticated the router's administrators, it could control Tier 0 and would have to be managed as Tier 0
quizzes.explanation: Anything that can control a Tier 0 system is Tier 0. Keeping NPS to port admission keeps SBD-DHCP01 in the member-server tier.

quizzes.question: Why does this lesson start 802.1X in monitor mode instead of enforcing it?
answers: Monitor mode is faster
The other 47 PCs have no machine certificate until they join the domain; enforcing now would strand them in VLAN 90, where they could never reach a domain controller
NPS cannot enforce on wired ports
quizzes.explanation: A PC enrolls its certificate only after it joins, and it can join only if the port lets it reach a domain controller. Monitor mode proves the configuration with the pilots without locking the rest of the fleet out.

recap: 802.1X runs on every VLAN 80 port in monitor mode: every result is logged, nothing is blocked yet.
The pilots authenticate with machine certificates; enforcement waits until the whole fleet has enrolled.
No new server: NPS runs on SBD-DHCP01, and its decisions are logged with everything else.
lessons.next: Lesson 6 scales from three machines to fifty, then switches the ports to enforcement.

lessons.title: Scale to fifty, enforce 802.1X, and prove by sample
lessons.summary: Roll the remaining waves while the ports are still in monitor mode, confirm every PC enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates, then switch the ports to enforcement — and prove the fleet the only honest way at scale: a defined sample, the same checks as the pilot, and a written rule for what a sample failure means.
objectives: Roll out the remaining endpoints in planned waves.
Confirm fleet-wide enrollment, then enforce 802.1X and prove an unenrolled device is quarantined.
Verify a defined sample against the pilot's full check set and enrol the fleet in event collection.
steps: Deploy the remaining machines in the planned waves while the VLAN 80 ports are still in monitor mode, adding each wave to SBD Fleet Computers from AdminJumpBox01 and restarting it so it enrolls, and watch the DHCP scope's utilization and the join events arriving in analysis as each wave lands — the pipeline is now the rollout's progress bar.

Confirm every PC enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates: compare the issuing CA's issued certificates and the NPS grant events (6272) against the fifty computer objects, and fix any machine that is missing before going further. Then retire course 1.7's temporary test client, SBD-TEST80, whose Tier 2 test role the pilots now carry: remove it from the domain, delete its computer object, lease and DNS records, and record the retirement.

Switch the VLAN 80 access ports from monitor mode to enforcement, and prove it both ways: an enrolled PC still authenticates and gets its normal lease, and an unenrolled test laptop lands in quarantine VLAN 90 and reaches nothing. Record the switch's port status and the NPS events for both.

Define the sample before checking it: for example one machine per wave plus any machine that logged an error — then run the pilot's full set on each sampled host (OU, policy, DNS, LAPS, certificate, 802.1X admission, peer-deny).
Write the sample rule down: one failed check in the sample widens the sample; a repeated failure stops the rollout and becomes a finding. A sample without a failure rule is a formality.

Enrol the fleet in course 1.10's collection: from AdminJumpBox01, add SBD Fleet Computers to SBD Event Sources and link course 1.10's enrolling GPO to the Workstations OU; from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, widen the collector's WinRM 5985 scope to VLAN 80 (rule F17); restart the PCs so both apply — and confirm fleet sign-ins now appear in the analyst's searches.
lessons.command:
(Get-ADComputer -SearchBase 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Filter *).Count   # 50, once SBD-TEST80 is retired
(Get-ADGroupMember 'SBD Fleet Computers').Count   # 50
# On SBD-DHCP01: authentication results in the last hour (6272 granted, 6273 denied).
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=6272,6273; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Group-Object Id | Select-Object Name, Count
Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -ScopeId 10.0.80.0 | Select-Object PercentageInUse, AddressesInUse
# On SBD-SYSLOG01: the fleet's events arriving
Get-WinEvent -LogName ForwardedEvents -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object MachineName, Id
lessons.check: Fifty computer objects sit in the Workstations OU and in SBD Fleet Computers, SBD-TEST80 is retired, every PC enrolled and authenticates, the ports enforce 802.1X with the unenrolled laptop quarantined in VLAN 90, scope utilization matches the rollout, every sampled host passes the full check set, and fleet events flow through the pipeline.
lessons.evidence: Keep the wave log, the enrollment reconciliation, the SBD-TEST80 retirement record, the enforcement change with both admission results and their records, the sample definition with its failure rule, the per-sample check results, and the enrolment proof from the collector.

quizzes.question: Why prove the fleet by sample instead of checking all fifty by hand?
answers: A defined sample with a failure rule is verifiable and honest at scale — and identical provenance is what the image hash bought you
Checking is impossible on Windows
Only pilots can be checked
quizzes.explanation: The factory model earns the sampling model. The written failure rule is what keeps the sample from being theater.

quizzes.question: What turns a sampled failure into more than a shrug?
answers: Deleting the failed machine
The written rule: failures widen the sample, repeats stop the rollout and become findings
Rebooting twice
quizzes.explanation: The rule was written before the checks ran — which is exactly what makes acting on it defensible.

quizzes.question: What is the pipeline's role during the rollout itself?
answers: It pauses to save disk
It only matters after completion
Live progress and anomaly surface — each wave's joins and errors appear as they happen
quizzes.explanation: The investment of courses 1.10–1.12 turns deployment into something observed, not something reconstructed afterward.

quizzes.question: When is it safe to switch the VLAN 80 ports from monitor mode to enforcement?
answers: As soon as the first pilot authenticates
Once every PC has enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates in monitor mode
Never; monitor mode is enough
quizzes.explanation: Enforce only after the whole fleet has proven it authenticates. Then a missing certificate cannot strand a machine in VLAN 90, and every unknown device that appears later is quarantined.

recap: Fifty machines, rolled in waves, watched as they landed.
Every PC enrolled before enforcement; an unenrolled device now lands in VLAN 90.
A defined sample with a failure rule carried the proof, and the fleet reports into the pipeline.
lessons.next: The final lesson baselines the fleet and hands off to courses 1.14 and 1.15.

lessons.title: Delta scan the fleet and hand off
lessons.summary: The cadence meets its first population: SBD-ADMIN-PC01 gets its own SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC) copy and its first baseline, the sampled endpoints get Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) baselines with the Windows client benchmark, the infrastructure this course changed is rescanned, and the fleet inventory is handed to course 1.15.
objectives: Install SCC on SBD-ADMIN-PC01 and baseline that seat, then the sampled endpoints, with the Windows client STIG benchmark.
Rescan the infrastructure this course touched.
Hand the fleet to courses 1.14 and 1.15.
steps: Install SBD-ADMIN-PC01's own SCC copy from course 1.4's media set, brought into the virtual machine on read-only media (an ISO image attached to its virtual DVD drive), checked against connected-side-hashes.csv and at the same version as the other seats' copies, and take that seat's first baseline with the Windows client benchmark — course 1.8 left it waiting for this copy.

Baseline the lesson 6 sample with the same benchmark from SBD-ADMIN-PC01. Rule A03 carries remote management, not the file-sharing and RPC ports a remote SCC scan uses, so copy SCC to each sampled PC over PowerShell remoting, check its hash there, scan locally in a Tier 2 session, bring the results back to C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\baseline, and remove SCC from the PC. Note how much the pre-linked policies and the OS defaults already satisfy, and classify open items the course 1.4 way.

Rescan what changed and attribute each delta to its lesson: the DCs (schema and LAPS attributes) and SBD-SUBCA01 (fleet enrollment volume) from AdminJumpBox01, and SBD-DHCP01 (the NPS role, its audit GPO and a scope in daily use) locally in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. Send any new deviation to the exception record's owner on AdminJumpBox01.
Assemble the fleet inventory — names, image ancestry, certificate thumbprints, sample status — as the course's closing artifact; course 1.15 makes it a source of SBD-MGMT01's living inventory.

Write the handoff: the fleet exists, watched and hardened, but takes no updates yet — course 1.14 builds SBD-WSUS01, with SBD-PC01–SBD-PC03 as its pilot ring and the other 47 PCs as Ring 2, and course 1.15 keeps the inventory current.
lessons.command:
# Inside SBD-ADMIN-PC01 (Tier 2), with the media set as D: (expected: True)
$scc = Get-Item 'D:\<SCC installer>'
(Get-FileHash $scc.FullName -Algorithm SHA256).Hash -in (Import-Csv D:\connected-side-hashes.csv).Hash
# Per sampled PC: carry the installer over remote management (A03), install and scan there, bring the results back
$s = New-PSSession SBD-PC07.sbd.test
Copy-Item $scc.FullName -ToSession $s -Destination C:\Windows\Temp\
Copy-Item '<SCC results folder on the PC>' -FromSession $s -Destination C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet\baseline\SBD-PC07 -Recurse
# After the scans: this seat's record, hashed
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\workstation-fleet-manifest.csv -NoTypeInformation
lessons.check: SBD-ADMIN-PC01 runs its own SCC copy with a dated first baseline, the sampled endpoints hold dated Windows client baselines with SCC removed afterwards, the infrastructure rescans carry attributed deltas, and the fleet inventory is complete and filed.
lessons.evidence: Finish the checklist: SBD-ADMIN-PC01's baseline, the endpoint baselines, infrastructure rescans, the fleet inventory, the hashed manifest, and the handoff note to courses 1.14 and 1.15.

CAs are rescanned weekly by rule
It was missed earlier
quizzes.explanation: The cadence follows change wherever it lands. Enrollment at fleet scale is a change worth measuring.

answers: Certificates and policy
Updates — SBD-WSUS01 arrives in course 1.14 — and an inventory kept current by course 1.15
Network addresses
quizzes.explanation: Honest handoffs name the gap. Fifty hardened machines that never patch would drift out of the state just proven — which is why course 1.14 is next.

recap: SBD-ADMIN-PC01 has its own SCC copy and baseline; the endpoints are baselined by sample.
Infrastructure deltas are attributed, and the fleet inventory is the closing artifact.
The gap — updates and a living inventory — is named for courses 1.14 and 1.15.
